 Medium

 Print Australia's David Warner, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith (Reuters Image) Former India all-rounder Irfan Pathan believes Australia's fresh ball-tampering scandal revelations could come back to haunt Pat Cummins and his team when they tour India for the Border-Gavaskar Trophy next year. With the controversy back in the spotlight following explosive claims by Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft, Pathan feels the Australian players will face considerable scrutiny from Indian fans and the media. The 2018 ball-tampering scandal, popularly known as 'Sandpapergate', has once again sparked debate after Khawaja and Bancroft suggested that knowledge of the controversial sandpaper tactic extended beyond the players who were directly punished. Their revelations have also raised fresh questions about collective responsibility within the Australian dressing room during the Test series against South Africa. Watch Yashasvi Jaiswal puts India on after bowlers show in Wellington While Cummins dismissed Khawaja's claims as "utter nonsense", Bancroft's detailed account in The West Australian offered further insight into the incident. The opener recalled discussions about reverse swing with Australia's bowlers, including Cummins, and claimed that his actions were encouraged, with several members of the team aware of the plan. Speaking on JioStar, Pathan said the fresh revelations would ensure that Australia remain under the scanner when they arrive in India for the five-match Border-Gavaskar Trophy series in January 2027. 'There will be a lot of talk': Irfan Pathan warns Australia ahead of India tour 
 Pathan believes the controversy will follow the Australian team throughout their India tour, with Cummins and his teammates needing to be mentally prepared to deal with questions surrounding the scandal. "I am pretty sure that when Australia comes down to India to play the BGT series, there will be a lot of talk around it. Wherever the Australians will go, they will have to face this. And they will have to be mentally strong to handle this, because it is all out there in the public domain," Pathan said. Pathan questions David Warner 's timing in addressing Sandpapergate 
 Pathan also questioned former Australia opener David Warner's decision to raise concerns about the investigation years after the incident. Warner, along with Steve Smith and Bancroft, was sanctioned following the scandal, with Warner receiving a leadership ban and a lifetime ban from holding a leadership position in Australian cricket. Pathan felt Warner should have spoken up at the time rather than questioning the investigation years later. He also pointed out that Cricket Australia's investigation had identified Warner, who was vice-captain at the time, as the player who initiated the plan to tamper with the ball. "I personally believe that Warner, because he has been through a ban, should have spoken then and there. Now, nothing can happen. The investigation happened over four days. Cricket Australia did what they thought was best at that particular time," he said. Join conversation

 "What I'm assuming from the investigation is that, because David Warner was the vice-captain, he was the one who initiated doing something with the ball. This is what the investigation by Cricket Australia established, and that's why it came out and he was punished. "Now, to talk about it and say that it was a shady investigation, I think it is too late. He should have spoken then and there, and things would have been very different," Pathan added.
